title: Lateran IV, 1215
hookLine: the council uses the word transubstantiation and asks Catholics to confess and receive at least yearly

lines: WHERE THE EASTER DUTY COMES FROM.
cards: Where does the phrase Easter duty come from? Some Catholics still use it: the yearly confession and communion around Easter, the floor below which you don't go.
It comes from a meeting of bishops at the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral church in Rome, called by the same Pope Innocent from yesterday's story.

Bishops and abbots came from across the West and wrote decrees on all sorts of things, but two lines from that meeting are still part of ordinary Catholic life. Today's word is Lateran IV, the fourth council held there.

teach.b: First line, about the altar. The council opens with a statement of faith, and it says that in the Mass the bread and wine are transubstantiated by divine power into Christ's body and blood.
That's the word transubstantiation, in a council's own text. The council didn't invent the belief.
Catholics read it in Jesus' words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed."
What the council did was give the belief a careful name: what the bread is changes, while what it looks like stays. Second line, about the heart.

Another decree says that every one of the faithful, man or woman, once they reach the age of discretion, should confess their sins faithfully at least once a year to their own priest, and receive communion with reverence at least at Easter.
Now notice the words at least.
This was never meant as the goal. It was a floor, a minimum for people who might otherwise drift for years: not once a year is enough, but don't go longer than this. Last, why it lasts.
The Church still keeps both lines as precepts of the Church: confess serious sins at least once a year, and receive communion at least during the Easter season.
Nothing stops a Catholic from going far more often. The floor is there for the years when life gets thin.

how: Catholic parishes post regular times for confession, and the precepts of the Church ask Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year and receive communion at least during the Easter season; Catholics may go far more often.

o: the council that first invented the belief in the Real Presence
a rule that every Catholic must go to confession each week
a council that named transubstantiation and set a yearly floor

p: the pope's cathedral church in Rome
the council's word for the change

s: Lateran IV invented the belief that the bread becomes Christ's body
Catholics read the belief in John's Gospel; the council gave it a careful name.
the council's yearly rule was meant as the ideal
it says at least: a floor for those who might drift, not a goal.
the yearly confession and Easter communion are still precepts of the Church
Catholics still keep both as minimums.

games.q: you're a bishop at the council. many people go years without confession or communion. what do you write?
o: set a floor: at least once a year, and communion at least at Easter.
leave it entirely to each person.
games.why: the council set a minimum, at least once a year, and the Church still keeps it as a precept.

practice: Think back to the last time you went to confession, or, if confession isn't part of your life, the last time you took an honest look at yourself, and notice the answer without judging it.
Then picture a real day and place for the next one, a parish schedule you could check, a quiet evening you could set aside, and let one or two things you'd bring rise to mind without digging.
If you pray, ask for the courage to keep the date.

wordCard.voice: Lateran IV. The fourth council at the Lateran in Rome, which named transubstantiation and set the yearly minimum for confession and Easter communion. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a change of substance — the council's canon speaks of bread and wine transubstantiated by divine power.

carryVoice: Your line: at least once a year. A floor to stand on, never a ceiling. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.
